item.title: PHP Releases Emergency Fixes for Critical PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities
item.description:
PHP releases emergency PHP2Shell fixes for two critical flaws allowing unauthenticated code execution. Website owners and hosting providers must update.

PHP developers have released emergency security updates for two critical vulnerabilities that can let attackers run code on web servers without logging in. The fixes arrived on October 21, 2026, a day after maintainers warned administrators to prepare for immediate patching.

Known publicly as PHP2Shell, the flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. PHP’s official announcement identifies installations serving web requests as at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed.

OpenAI said cybersecurity firm Calif identified a critical PHP flaw using GPT-5.6 Sol through its Patch the Planet initiative. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with support from the researchers and infrastructure providers.

However, Calif later credited independent researcher @lcfr_hax with first finding PHP2Shell and developing a working exploit. The company said his work persuaded the PHP Foundation to fund fixes for the entire class of bugs and that he helped review and repeatedly test the patches.

Apache mod_php Faces the Highest Risk

PHP maintainers consider Apache’s mod_php setup the highest-risk deployment because researchers demonstrated an attack that works before the website’s own code begins running.

An attacker exploiting the flaws gains the permissions of the process handling web requests. That access can expose application files and credentials available to that process, although it does not automatically grant administrator privileges over the entire server.

Shahak Shalev, Global Head of Scam and AI Research at Malwarebytes, described how attackers could abuse a compromised website’s existing reputation.

“This is a goldmine for hackers. They can hijack real websites to take advantage of the site’s reputation to do things like phish people, serve malicious software from the trusted channel; the opportunities are endless,” Shalev said.

PHP’s advisories describe different attack conditions depending on the server configuration, application and installed extensions.

Errors in Memory Handling Allow Code Execution

The first vulnerability, CVE-2026-109618, affects how PHP handles running out of memory. Processing can stop while internal request data is only partly prepared, leaving PHP’s cleanup routines to use invalid data. Researchers confirmed remote code execution against Apache mod_php under default PHP input and memory limits.

The second flaw, CVE-2026-109619, allows information from an earlier request to remain referenced after its memory has been released. A later request handled by the same worker process can act on those references, enabling memory disclosure or code execution.

Researchers validated attacks against both mod_php and PHP-FPM, although the confirmed FPM route requires a suitable operation within the application. PHP’s advisory warns that running multiple workers reduces the success rate per request but does not remove the vulnerability.

Emergency Updates Are Available

Administrators should install the fixed release for their PHP branch.

Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance. Organisations using vendor-maintained packages should check the corresponding security notice for confirmation that the fixes are included.

PHP 8.1 and older are outside the project’s normal support period. Maintainers have also supplied minimal source patches for PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, while users of older installations should consult their vendor or move to a supported release.

Website owners using managed hosting should ask their provider to confirm that the PHP runtime has been patched. Updating WordPress, its plugins or themes does not replace the server’s PHP installation.

Configuration Changes Offer Incomplete Protection

Administrators unable to patch immediately can consult the official advisories for temporary controls. These include disabling session upload progress and, on PHP 8.5, disabling fatal-error backtraces, followed by restarting every PHP worker.

Those changes block specific demonstrated attack paths. PHP maintainers warn that no generic configuration change covers every route, and hiding error messages does not prevent exploitation of the stale-state vulnerability. Installing the complete fixes remains necessary.

Waqas
I am a UK-based cybersecurity journalist with a passion for covering the latest happenings in cybersecurity and tech world. I am also into gaming, reading and investigative journalism.

item.title: Arrakis Security Report Finds 76% of AI Agents Are Dormant but Keep Their Credentials and Connections
item.description:
New York, NY, USA, October 21st, 2026, CyberNewswire

According to the 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report, published by Arrakis Security, 76% of active agents have not run in 60 days, but their credentials still work and their triggers still fire. 44% have not run in 180 days. 24% of dormant agents can be started by an unsigned webhook from outside the organization.

The report is based on anonymized, unidentifiable production telemetry from thousands of AI agents in Arrakis customers’ environments, collected over a 12-week period.

“There’s a lot of discussion about AI agent risk, and very little data”, said Tal Baron, CEO and co-founder of Arrakis Security. “When an employee leaves, their access is removed the same day. When an agent stops being used, nobody removes anything, because in most companies nobody owns it”.

﻿Other findings:

  • 22% of agents can send content to a model run by a third party and act on the answer.
  • 20% of agents can pass a task to another agent with different permissions, and get back results they aren’t allowed to produce themselves.
  • 70% of agents can reach sensitive systems, such as cloud storage, AI services, and marketing platforms, and almost none of those connections have verified data loss prevention (DLP).
  • 82% of agents carry at least one exposure, and 46% of those carry more than one.

The full report is available at https://arrakis.security/2026-threat-report.

About Arrakis Security

Arrakis secures autonomous agents through behavioral intelligence across three layers: what an agent is, what it does, and why. AI-SPM scans each agent’s structure, permissions, tools, and metadata hourly, including agents that never run, surfacing shadow agents, exposed keys, and misconfigurations. AI-TDR monitors actions in real time for deviations from defined rules and policies. The behavioral intelligence engine models each agent from its own history, posture, runtime, and context: how it got there and what it could do next. For each action, it decides whether to continue, escalate, or intervene.

Contact

Moranne Shechnick
Arrakis Security

item.title: Qilin and INC Exploit Palo Alto VPN Flaw in Ransomware Attacks
item.description:
Qilin and INC ransomware operators exploit a PAN-OS vulnerability (CVE-2026-0257) to gain VPN access, then steal domain credentials from VMware virtual disks.

After exploiting a vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS software to gain VPN access, attackers started targeting virtual server infrastructure and extracted domain credentials from a domain controller’s virtual disk, according to the company’s Unit 42 threat intelligence team’s latest research blog.

The incident is part of ongoing exploitation of CVE-2026-0257, an authentication-bypass flaw affecting the GlobalProtect portal and gateway. The vulnerability can allow attackers to establish VPN sessions by bypassing authentication controls, even multi-factor authentication (MFA).

In updates published on October 19 and 20, Unit 42 identified Qilin, also known as Spikey Scorpius, and Inc, aka Tarnished Scorpius, among the ransomware operators exploiting the flaw. Separate reports have linked exploitation to actors using Settra ransomware. CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026.

From VPN Access to Domain Credentials

Unit 42’s investigations, which began in early June, found attackers using remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools to survey internal networks before moving between systems over Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) and Server Message Block (SMB).

The research covered organizations across 11 sectors, including education, financial services, healthcare, high technology, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and wholesale and retail.

In one investigated credential-theft incident, attackers reached VMware’s vCenter management appliance, disabled the execInstalledOnly security control on ESXi hypervisors and used a custom tool to extract credentials offline from a domain controller’s virtual machine disk (VMDK).

Working directly with the virtual disk allowed the attackers to avoid endpoint detection and response (EDR) controls running inside the guest operating system. Unit 42 also observed attackers using exploit tools targeting Veeam backup infrastructure, including those exploiting CVE-2023-27532.

This vulnerability affects Veeam Backup & Replication and can expose encrypted credentials stored in its configuration database, potentially giving attackers access to backup infrastructure. Hackread previously reported that ransomware groups including Akira and FIN7 had exploited the flaw.

Exposed Management Interfaces

Unit 42 also found misconfigured GlobalProtect profiles exposing management interfaces to the internet on ports 4443 and 3879. Administrators should check whether these interfaces are externally accessible and follow Palo Alto Networks’ guidance to restrict access.

The findings also provide context for a separate VMware vCenter campaign covered by Hackread.com in August, when researchers linked 361 IP addresses across 47 countries to suspected exploitation of CVE-2026-59310. The vulnerabilities and campaigns differ, but both highlight the risks of attackers reaching virtualization management systems.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: Gcore Makes Enterprise Security Bundle Free for Public Agencies Until End of the Year
item.description:
Contern, Luxembourg, October 22nd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Gcore is offering its WAAP Enterprise plan free of charge to any government body or public agency until December 31, 2026. The offer follows the php2shell vulnerabilities that forced public websites offline across Europe earlier this week.

Gcore WAAP blocks the php2shell attack path (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) by default for all customers. Sites taken offline can be placed behind the service and brought back online while patching continues. The two PHP vulnerabilities, rated CVSS 9.2, allow unauthenticated remote code execution before any application code runs. Government portals in the Netherlands, Finland, Denmark, and France, along with hospitals, schools, and commercial sites, were taken offline this week on the advice of CERT-EU and national agencies.

Going offline was the right call while no fix existed. Patching large estates takes days. A filtering layer that blocks the attack pattern lets a site run while that work is done. If new variants appear, Gcore updates the rule centrally and operators do not need to repeat the patching cycle.

Gcore’s Enterprise plan covers domains and websites, custom rules, IP reputation, bot management, threat intelligence, API security, and SIEM integration. Public-sector organizations can apply here with an official government domain.

Gcore advises all PHP operators to update to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35; restart PHP-FPM and long-running workers after updating; and restrict origin access so traffic reaches the server only through a protection layer. PHP 8.1 and older receive no official fix; operators should obtain a vendor backport or upgrade.

About Gcore

Gcore connects the world to AI, anywhere, anytime. As a leading-edge platform provider of AI, cloud, network, and security solutions, Gcore helps businesses industry-wide to deliver fast, secure, and seamless experiences for their customers, no matter where they’re located.

Gcore solutions accelerate AI training and deployment, deliver efficient, customizable cloud services, improve content delivery, and protect servers, web applications, and APIs. Leveraging extensive, flexible, global edge infrastructure, Gcore products can scale with business needs, enabling organizations to drive AI innovation, push the boundaries of technology, and reach their potential while maintaining the fundamentals: operational efficiency, consistency, and control.

Join thousands of businesses worldwide, including Orange, Wargaming, Xsolla, and Avast, using Gcore as the foundation for their global infrastructure, applications, and business.

Learn more at www.gcore.com and follow us on LinkedIn, X, YouTube, and Facebook.

Contact

PR & Communications Lead
Daniel Hoelzer
Gcore

item.title: Operation Serengeti III Nets 1,462 Arrests and $105M in Cybercrime Crackdown
item.description:
INTERPOL’s Operation Serengeti III targeted cybercrime in 21 African countries, recovering over $105 million and identifying 65,929 victims of criminal networks.

INTERPOL-coordinated Operation Serengeti III has resulted in 1,462 arrests, the disruption of 10,909 malicious networks, and the recovery of more than $105 million in illicit funds. The operation targeted cybercrime networks across Africa, with cybersecurity firms Group-IB and Team Cymru providing intelligence to support investigations. Both companies shared details of their contributions with Hackread.com.

Conducted between June 29 and August 31, 2026, the operation involved law enforcement agencies from 21 countries. Investigators identified 65,929 victims and linked criminal activity to financial losses exceeding $385 million.

Fraud and Cryptocurrency Crime Across Africa

In Uganda, authorities dismantled two transnational fraud rings and arrested 365 foreign nationals linked to investment and pension scams targeting victims in Asia. Investigators uncovered call centers using scripted communications and fake trading platforms.

In Angola, authorities dismantled two illegal cryptocurrency mining centers, arrested nine suspects and seized more than 2,000 mining devices and six illegal power transformation stations. The electrical infrastructure alone was valued at over $1 million.

In Nigeria, authorities arrested a suspect linked to a phishing and business email compromise (BEC) operation involving approximately 2.1 million email addresses and harvested software credentials. A separate investigation uncovered more than $2.4 million in suspected criminal proceeds, much of it laundered through cryptocurrency.

Other actions targeted a malicious mobile lending application scheme in Tanzania, a vehicle import fraud network in Gabon and 30 suspects in the Republic of Congo.

Group-IB and Team Cymru Contribute Threat Intelligence

According to Group-IB’s press release, it supplied INTERPOL with intelligence on phishing kits, botnets and other malicious resources hosted in Africa or used in attacks targeting the region. It also shared information on suspected fraudsters, including social media accounts linked to their activities.

“Operation Serengeti III demonstrates the importance of sustained cooperation between law enforcement and the private sector,” stated Dmitry Volkov, Group-IB’s CEO, highlighting how threat intelligence and coordinated investigations can help disrupt criminal networks.

Team Cymru contributed intelligence on suspicious domains, IP addresses and command-and-control infrastructure. Its analysis of internet infrastructure helps investigators identify connections between systems and build a broader picture of criminal operations.

“Criminals cannot operate without infrastructure. They have to build it, connect it and maintain it, and those activities create opportunities to find them,” stated Jacomo Piccolini, Team Cymru’s vice president of global data partnerships.

“Operation Serengeti III reinforces a clear message: while cybercrime is increasingly borderless, international cooperation remains one of the most effective tools for disrupting criminal networks, recovering criminal assets and protecting communities from digital harm,” said Neal Jetton, INTERPOL’s director of cybercrime.

Operation Serengeti III also received support from Kaspersky, Fortinet, TrendAI, Uppsala Security, Cybercrime Atlas, Meta, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance and Zimbabwe’s Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority.

The operation builds on INTERPOL’s earlier efforts under the Serengeti initiative. In 2024, the original Operation Serengeti resulted in 1,006 arrests and the dismantling of more than 134,000 malicious infrastructures and networks, as previously reported by Hackread.com. Operation Serengeti 2.0, conducted in 2025, resulted in 1,209 arrests, the disruption of 11,432 malicious networks and the recovery of $97.4 million.

item.title: Paying in ADA: Cardano’s vision for the future of payroll
item.description:
The crypto economy is maturing faster than the bulk of traditional organizations could’ve imagined. In light of this financial revolution, payroll is emerging as one of its most powerful use cases. Crypto’s role in today’s economy extends from trading to enterprise remuneration and international settlements, and its influence is growing, with trends tracked by all sorts of online outlets, such as Binance News.

Cardano, the blockchain platform on which its native cryptocurrency ADA runs, is increasingly positioned as a credible foundation for real-world financial systems. Freelancers, businesses, and decentralized organizations, also referred to as DAOs (decentralized autonomous organizations), are opening up to the idea of compensation that’s borderless, programmable, and more efficient than traditional banking systems.

In today’s digital-first environment, where innovation outpaces regulations, Cardano offers an architecture designed for long-term reliability, built on peer-reviewed research, energy-efficient proof-of-stake, and formal verification, which push it beyond the hype that can often accompany crypto and blockchain projects.

Financial discussions range from enterprise adoption to ADA price predictions, the latter of which partially reflects the feelings of investors worldwide regarding the broader project. And right now, observers are evaluating how Cardano could influence remuneration models in the future and why it matters for payroll systems around the world.

Cardano’s emergence in crypto payroll

Cardano managed to stand out from the crypto crowd by leveraging a layered approach to its development, with papers published in academic journals and reviewed by crypto experts, alongside distributed systems and computer science, serving as a foundation.

Its peer-review process allows independent academics and developers to scrutinize designs, thereby improving trustworthiness and reducing reliance on a single team’s judgment and removing bias. Such quality resonates deeply with organizations looking for infrastructures designed for durability, sustainability, and auditability.

Employees rely on accuracy, timelines, and transparency, so payroll can no longer be something organizations test on the fly; it demands a reliable, robust system built for real-world use.

As crypto salaries become more visible, with employment sources like recruitment platforms urging or requiring companies to inform visitors about the potential remuneration they can expect after a deal, a structural change emerges in how compensation can work in decentralized environments.

So instead of a one-direction, monthly transaction, blockchain transforms payroll into a programmable process that supports automation and global settlement in a transparent, secure way.

Cardano’s governance philosophy and the rising number of developers position it as an appealing platform for builders creating payroll tools, HR integrations, and financial apps.

Tech developments

Cardano’s roadmap focuses on scalability, security, and governance. Hydra, for instance, is the network’s layer-2 protocol and helps support a high number of transactions while keeping costs down and maintaining the network’s integrity – particularly relevant feats for payroll scenarios where large teams and recurrent payments are involved.

The Voltaire phase, on the other hand, introduces decentralized governance and allows ADA investors and holders to become part of the network’s evolution, which is of particular importance since the payroll system should be trusted over a long timeframe.

Transparent decision-making and community funding mechanisms are key in creating enterprise-level tools like automated vesting systems, milestone-based payouts, and auditable smart contracts, to name a few. The result? A foundation capable of supporting both startups and institutions, complex or simple alike, with tools designed for reliability and scalability.

Macroeconomic forces

Some of the most powerful factors shaping how organizations feel about crypto, whether it’s ADA, BTC, ETH, XRP, LTC, and so forth, are macroeconomic conditions that strongly impact the crypto industry’s integration into the financial world – compensation ecosystem included. From inflation to interest rates and from liquidity pools to the broader capital market sentiment, all play a role in how risk-averse or tolerant a company can be.

At the same time, governments are gradually clarifying tax treatment and accounting requirements. In the U.S., for instance, the IRS treats crypto as property when it comes to taxes, and requires investors and holders to report both gains and losses, while in Germany, crypto held for over a year can be exempt from capital gains tax.

Evolving rules impact the way organizations design payroll strategies involving digital assets directly, and they’re key developments to follow to better understand where parts of the broader financial system is heading. Companies that consider Cardano-supported payroll must align their operations with these realities and address aspects like how they’ll navigate the volatility of the crypto industry in advance.

Stablecoins emerge as a bridge

Stablecoins, as the name suggests, are digital assets created with the scope of being more stable compared to Bitcoin, altcoins, utility coins, and so forth – and that’s why their value is pegged to assets like fiat money (USD, EUR, GBP), or commodities like gold and silver. Cardano is integrating USDC stablecoins into its ecosystem, an undertaking that’s expected to improve community engagement, change decentralized finance, and help fintech organizations tackle regulatory hurdles more easily. Cardano supports a number of stablecoins, USDM, DJED, and USDA, that can be used to make transactions on supported platforms.

The project’s current focus is on developing decentralized stablecoins and robust settlement layers, initiatives that could help reduce volatility risk while maintaining fast transaction settlement and programmability. The key question for organizations and developers becomes whether the operational benefits outweigh the governance and oversight responsibilities needed to manage digital assets securely.

Real-world adoption

Crypto payroll is already being tested across software companies, web3 organizations, creative collectives, remote teams, and so forth. Cross-border contributors benefit from faster settlement and fewer intermediaries, leveraging automated smart contracts that support transparent grants, rewards, and recurring compensation.

However, success is heavily reliant on user experience, education, and custodial security. Finance leaders must coordinate with tax advisors and auditors, and employees must gain a solid understanding of custody, taxes, and wallet management, to name a few developments. Cardano’s advantage, nevertheless, lies in its patient, standards-driven ecosystem that’s focused on building mature tooling rather than chasing trends.

Cardano is steadily growing into a reliable blockchain payroll solution, and it may redefine global compensation, merging speed, transparency, and compliance for businesses everywhere. Will you be here to watch payroll transform?

item.title: 426 Android and iOS Apps Linked to PHP2Shell Backend Risks
item.description:
Research found 426 mobile apps connecting to servers advertising PHP versions potentially affected by PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, raising concerns about backend security.

NowSecure has identified 426 Android and iOS apps connecting to servers that report versions of PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor), a programming language used to build websites and backend services, affected by the recently patched PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.

In research shared with Hackread.com, the cybersecurity firm urged developers to check the servers supporting their apps, including those operated by outside providers. The reported versions alone do not confirm whether a server remains unpatched or can be exploited.

PHP2Shell Flaws Raise Backend Security Concerns

The PHP project released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, on October 21, 2026, each rated CVSS v4.0 9.2. Hackread.com reported on the emergency PHP2Shell fixes, which address flaws that can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers.

For context, both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities were first identified by independent researcher @lcfr_hax. The flaws affect PHP running on the servers that mobile apps contact, not software installed on users’ phones. Servers using Apache’s mod_php component, which runs PHP within the web server, face particular risk because an attack can succeed before the website’s own code starts running.

Wiz Research also demonstrated how AI models could help develop working exploit chains for the flaws. NowSecure’s research examined how many mobile apps were connecting to servers that could still be vulnerable.

8.5% of Assessed Apps Connected to Potentially Vulnerable Servers

NowSecure’s findings analysed 15,429 mobile apps and found that 454 connected to servers that disclosed their PHP versions. Of those apps, 426, or 93.8%, contacted servers running potentially affected versions. Of those 426 apps, 170 connected to servers running end-of-life PHP branches that no longer receive official upstream security updates.

The company also reported in its blog that 8.5% of assessed apps connected to at least one potentially vulnerable PHP server. This does not mean those servers were all exploitable or remained unpatched.

The findings also show how a single backend can affect many apps. One advertising vendor’s server was contacted by 151 apps, while 88% of the identified PHP servers served just one app, often through a developer’s own backend. Fixing the issue can therefore depend on whether the server belongs to the app developer or an outside provider.

Developers Need to Identify Who Runs Their Servers

Some apps connect to PHP servers through third-party advertising or analytics tools. In these cases, developers may not know who operates every server their apps contact. They will need to work with those providers to confirm whether the affected PHP versions have been updated.

NowSecure plans to add a feature to its platform that identifies apps connecting to servers that report potentially affected PHP versions. Developers will still need to check with the server owner to confirm whether the fixes have been applied.

Teams are advised to “treat the finding as an infrastructure and application security incident,” and update affected servers to PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 or 8.5.12. Those running PHP 8.1 or older should move to a supported branch or check if their vendor has released a fixed package. It is also important to review server logs for signs of exploitation and possible exposure of credentials or access tokens.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: When It Makes Sense to Replace a Legacy Virtualization Stack
item.description:
Virtualization platforms often remain in place long after their original purpose because migration carries operational risk. Yet aging architecture creates visible costs through licensing changes, specialist skills, slow upgrades, and limited deployment choices.

A replacement makes sense when those pressures outweigh the effort of moving users and applications. The decision needs evidence from daily administration, infrastructure plans, and user requirements. Several practical signals show when a legacy stack has reached that point.

Signs The Stack Has Aged

Organizations should first examine how much work it takes to keep the current environment available. Repeated configuration tasks, separate management consoles, and specialist training consume administrator time.

Research into Citrix alternatives helps decision-makers compare management models, deployment paths, licensing structures, and support requirements before a replacement project begins. That comparison turns general frustration into measurable selection criteria.

Frequent delays also indicate technical debt. If routine updates require extensive testing across several components, the platform consumes time that IT teams could spend on security or service improvements.

A stack that depends on aging hardware creates another warning sign. Replacement planning becomes urgent when storage, servers, or network appliances approach support limits, especially if the existing design requires proprietary dependencies.

Rising Costs Change The Decision

Licensing expenses provide a clear reason to review the current platform. Costs increase when an environment requires separate components for gateway access, monitoring, load balancing, reporting, or user management.

Maintenance labor matters just as much. A platform that needs specialized administrators, recurring training, and lengthy troubleshooting carries a higher total cost of ownership than its license invoice suggests.

Finance teams should compare the full operating model across several years. Include software licenses, infrastructure refreshes, support contracts, training, administrative labor, and the cost of delayed changes.

Limited Deployment Choices

A legacy stack often becomes restrictive when an organization adopts hybrid infrastructure. Teams might need to keep existing on-premises workloads while placing selected applications in cloud services.

The replacement should support both environments with a single management approach. Parallels RAS provides on-premises deployment, hybrid access, and direct integration with the Azure Virtual Desktop control plane.

This structure helps organizations preserve current investments while moving workloads in stages. It also avoids forcing every application into the same hosting model before business requirements justify that change.

User Requirements Have Changed

Work patterns provide another test. Employees now access applications from laptops, tablets, thin clients, and personal devices, often outside a corporate office.

A suitable platform must publish desktops and applications across those devices without creating separate administrative processes. It should also handle printing, session access, and user authentication through a consistent workspace.

Performance complaints deserve careful investigation. Slow logins, unreliable sessions, or inconsistent application access can indicate capacity issues, poor gateway design, or a platform that no longer fits current usage.

Build a Replacement Case

A replacement project needs measurable acceptance criteria before technical evaluation begins. Useful measures include deployment time, administrator steps, support tickets, licensing components, session reliability, and application launch performance.

The team should inventory every published application, user group, policy, integration, and dependency. This inventory identifies workloads that need testing and prevents overlooked requirements from delaying migration.

Pilot testing should begin with a controlled user group and representative applications. Administrators can then compare login behavior, printing, access policies, reporting, and support effort against the existing environment.

Parallels RAS includes a single management console, built-in monitoring and reporting, universal printing, and a single licensing model. Those functions address common reasons organizations review an older virtualization stack.

Conclusion

Replacing a legacy virtualization stack makes sense when operating effort, licensing demands, infrastructure limits, or user problems exceed the platform’s practical value. The next step is a documented assessment, not an immediate migration.

Record current components, annual costs, administrative tasks, application dependencies, and deployment goals. Then test a replacement with representative users and workloads. A measured pilot gives decision-makers evidence about performance, support effort, and total cost before a wider transition begins.

item.title: Overlord RAT Uses Fake Legal Notices to Infect Windows PCs in New Campaign
item.description:
WatchGuard details Overlord RAT attacks using fake Brazilian legal notices, plus Lampion malware and a separate remote access campaign targeting users in Portugal.

Overlord RAT has surfaced in a newly documented malware campaign discovered by WatchGuard that uses fake Brazilian legal notices to trick victims into downloading malicious files. The RAT has previously been reported by Hackread.com in campaigns involving a fake Zoom installer targeting Windows and macOS, and malicious npm packages used to distribute it alongside an information stealer.

In research shared with Hackread.com, WatchGuard Red Cell researcher Euler Neto identified eight fraudulent domains impersonating Brazilian notary offices. The campaign uses obfuscated VBScript, trusted cloud storage services and legitimate Windows applications to deliver the remote access trojan (RAT), while the wider investigation examines two other malware campaigns targeting users in Portugal.

Overlord RAT Exploits Fake Legal Notices

The campaign uses phishing emails posing as Brazilian protest notary offices. The eight domains include 1protestorecife.com and cartorioquintela.com. Links in the emails incorporate valid CNPJ numbers, Brazil’s national registry numbers for legal entities, to make the notices appear legitimate.

Clicking a link downloads an obfuscated VBScript that retrieves additional files from Dropbox or Google Cloud Storage. The scripts use Windows tools such as PowerShell and curl to download payloads, while some modify Microsoft Defender exclusions to reduce the likelihood of detection.

The infection chain also abuses legitimate applications, including Microsoft’s .NET Framework executable ngentask.exe and the VLC media player, to load malicious DLLs. Another variant creates scheduled tasks named “Windows Error Reporting” to maintain persistence.

A Go-based executable downloads an encrypted file named werdata.db and decrypts its contents using the Chaskey cipher in counter mode. Researchers identified the decrypted content as Donut x64 shellcode. The malware then communicates with Overlord RAT infrastructure at 191.96.225.125 and 45.158.8.213, which the report associates with port 5173.

The researchers also found references to Brazilian financial institutions, including C6Bank, PicPay, Banco Inter and Caixa Econômica Federal, in the malware.

Lampion and a Separate Remote Access Campaign

The second campaign delivers the Lampion banking trojan through phishing emails containing ZIP attachments with HTML files. These files retrieve additional scripts hosted on services such as AWS S3 or Google Drive. The heavily obfuscated VBScript stages contain junk code that complicates analysis, while the observed command-and-control infrastructure includes Russian-based IP addresses.

The third campaign uses a Portuguese-language website titled “Download Seguro – Factura” and a fake CAPTCHA to distribute an ISO file. The ISO contains a VBScript, VMware’s legitimate vnetlib.exe and a malicious newdev.dll.

When vnetlib.exe loads the DLL, the malicious code decrypts another 64-bit DLL payload written in Pascal. The payload can execute commands, transfer files, control the mouse and keyboard, and stream the victim’s screen. It also adds a Windows registry entry to maintain access after a system restart.

Although the three campaigns use different infection methods, they rely on familiar tricks to get malware onto victims’ systems, from fake legal notices and phishing emails carrying financial or administrative lures to a bogus invoice-download page.

The use of cloud storage and legitimate applications also gives security teams more than suspicious files to investigate, including unexpected script activity, changes to Defender exclusions and unusual network connections.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: GoDaddy Revokes 404,607 SSL Certificates After Policy Errors
item.description:
GoDaddy revoked 404,607 SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates on October 21, 2026, after finding errors in how they had been issued. The affected certificates were issued under GoDaddy and Starfield.

The issue came to light after a third party found that the certificates did not match Starfield’s published Certificate Policy and Certification Practice Statement (CP/CPS). The differences involved certificate policy object identifiers (OIDs) and CPS URI qualifiers, which identify the policies associated with a certificate and point to the authority’s documented practices.

GoDaddy suspended certificate issuance while investigating, corrected its published documentation and resumed issuance. Its review also identified similar discrepancies in the older Starfield G2 hierarchy, which no longer issued new certificates, according to Mozilla’s incident report.

Domain-validation (DV) certificates accounted for most of the affected population. Starfield R1 DV accounted for 208,896 certificates, while Starfield G2 DV accounted for 187,159. Another 8,552 organization-validation (OV) and extended-validation (EV) certificates were affected across the listed certificate hierarchies.

GoDaddy Missed Its Revocation Deadline

The CA/Browser Forum’s TLS Baseline Requirements state that affected certificates should be revoked within 24 hours and must be revoked within five days, subject to exceptions.

GoDaddy began contacting affected customers on October 14 but missed its October 18 deadline at 23:45 UTC. By then, only 170,566 certificates had been revoked. The total reached 227,422 by 05:29 UTC on October 19, according to Mozilla’s delayed-revocation report. GoDaddy’s customer guidance subsequently confirmed that the affected certificates were revoked on October 21.

In its customer guidance notice, the company warns that websites may display security warnings or become inaccessible until a replacement certificate is installed. Its dashboard identifies certificates requiring action, including cases where a new certificate is available but the website is still using the revoked one. GoDaddy also provides an SSL Status Check tool for verifying a certificate’s current status.

What Website Owners Should Do

The problem has reached Gibraltar’s government websites. On October 22, the government confirmed that some sites were using affected certificates and its IT team was working to replace them. Visitors were told not to ignore browser security warnings or enter personal or payment details on affected pages.

“An error by GoDaddy, one of the companies that issues website security certificates worldwide, has affected some HM Government of Gibraltar websites.”

“Visitors to these sites may see a security warning in their browser, or may be unable to open the site, until a replacement certificate is in place,” official notification from the Government of Gibraltar noted.

Website owners should check their GoDaddy accounts for certificates flagged for replacement. They also need to check the live website: downloading a replacement does not install it automatically. If the server continues presenting the revoked certificate, visitors may still encounter security warnings or connection errors.

The incident follows another certificate-related security case covered by Hackread.com in May, when attackers obtained DigiCert code-signing certificates and used them to sign malware. In the GoDaddy case, the published disclosures concern certificate-policy discrepancies and do not establish private-key theft or a compromise of TLS encryption.

Certificate Revocation Highlights Need for Automation

Chris Hickman, Chief Security Officer at Keyfactor, shared his comments with Hackread.com on the GoDaddy incident and the importance of certificate management.

“The reason GoDaddy had to revoke more than 400,000 certificates is that there was a mismatch between the way the certificates were issued and the documentation that backs that up — their Certificate Policy and Certification Practice Statement, or CP/CPS. That requires them to revoke the certificates and reissue them as per the CA Browser Forum who oversees the guidelines that govern publicly rooted certificates like those issued by GoDaddy. So, this is actually a documentation error that led to this.

“The thing I really want to point to is that, of all the certificates that needed to be replaced, those that were automated simplified the job. However, for those that were not, the owners of those systems may not even realize that their certificates have been revoked and could be suffering an outage.

“This really does clarify the need to be agile with certificate management and the automation of certificates, and to have the visibility to understand when an event like this impacts certificates that have been issued to you.

“The guidance is: if you have certificates in your environment issued by one of the impacted certificate authorities, you need to confirm with GoDaddy whether your certificates are affected and, if they have been revoked, obtain the new certificate for the affected systems.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

GoDaddy revoked 404,607 SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and TLS (Transport Layer Security) certificates on October 21, 2026, after finding errors in how they had been issued. The affected certificates were issued under GoDaddy and Starfield.

The issue came to light after a third party found that the certificates did not match Starfield’s published Certificate Policy and Certification Practice Statement (CP/CPS). The differences involved certificate policy object identifiers (OIDs) and CPS URI qualifiers, which identify the policies associated with a certificate and point to the authority’s documented practices.

GoDaddy suspended certificate issuance while investigating, corrected its published documentation and resumed issuance. Its review also identified similar discrepancies in the older Starfield G2 hierarchy, which no longer issued new certificates, according to Mozilla’s incident report.

Domain-validation (DV) certificates accounted for most of the affected population. Starfield R1 DV accounted for 208,896 certificates, while Starfield G2 DV accounted for 187,159. Another 8,552 organization-validation (OV) and extended-validation (EV) certificates were affected across the listed certificate hierarchies.

GoDaddy Missed Its Revocation Deadline

The CA/Browser Forum’s TLS Baseline Requirements state that affected certificates should be revoked within 24 hours and must be revoked within five days, subject to exceptions.

GoDaddy began contacting affected customers on October 14 but missed its October 18 deadline at 23:45 UTC. By then, only 170,566 certificates had been revoked. The total reached 227,422 by 05:29 UTC on October 19, according to Mozilla’s delayed-revocation report. GoDaddy’s customer guidance subsequently confirmed that the affected certificates were revoked on October 21.

In its customer guidance notice, the company warns that websites may display security warnings or become inaccessible until a replacement certificate is installed. Its dashboard identifies certificates requiring action, including cases where a new certificate is available but the website is still using the revoked one. GoDaddy also provides an SSL Status Check tool for verifying a certificate’s current status.

What Website Owners Should Do

The problem has reached Gibraltar’s government websites. On October 22, the government confirmed that some sites were using affected certificates and its IT team was working to replace them. Visitors were told not to ignore browser security warnings or enter personal or payment details on affected pages.

“An error by GoDaddy, one of the companies that issues website security certificates worldwide, has affected some HM Government of Gibraltar websites.”

“Visitors to these sites may see a security warning in their browser, or may be unable to open the site, until a replacement certificate is in place,” official notification from the Government of Gibraltar noted.

Website owners should check their GoDaddy accounts for certificates flagged for replacement. They also need to check the live website: downloading a replacement does not install it automatically. If the server continues presenting the revoked certificate, visitors may still encounter security warnings or connection errors.

The incident follows another certificate-related security case covered by Hackread.com in May, when attackers obtained DigiCert code-signing certificates and used them to sign malware. In the GoDaddy case, the published disclosures concern certificate-policy discrepancies and do not establish private-key theft or a compromise of TLS encryption.
